lessons.title: Early-Stage Valuation Methods: Scorecard, Berkus, VC Method and Comparables

children.text: If P/E and DCF do not work for startups, how does anyone arrive at a number? Not with one perfect formula. Early-stage investors use a handful of simple, openly subjective methods, run several of them, and see where the answers cluster. In this lesson you will value one fictional Indore startup four different ways and learn what each method is good for, where it misleads, and how to use the results when a founder hands you a valuation.

body.text: No early-stage valuation method gives you the answer. Each gives you a defensible range. Run several, look for overlap, and treat any single number as the start of a negotiation, not a fact.

children.text: The Startup We Will Value
VidyaSetu Learning Private Limited is a fictional Indore startup running a Hindi-medium test preparation app for state government job exams. It is raising a ₹2 crore seed round.

cells: Live Android app with mock tests and recorded lessons
Ex-coaching institute founder plus a product lead from a funded edtech
Content tie-ups with two coaching institutes in Madhya Pradesh
Crowded, with several well-funded national test-prep apps

children.text: Method 1: The Berkus Method

Angel investor Dave Berkus designed this method in the 1990s for startups with little or no revenue. Instead of forecasting, you assign a value to each of five things that reduce risk, up to a fixed cap per element. The original cap was $500,000 per element. For this lesson we use an illustrative Indian cap of ₹1 crore each, so the maximum pre-money valuation is ₹5 crore.

body.caption: Berkus valuation of VidyaSetu (cap ₹1 crore per element)

cells: Large, clearly underserved Hindi-medium exam market
Relevant founders, but no prior exit

body.text: Berkus is quick and forces you to name the risks, but the per-element cap is arbitrary, and the method was built for pre-revenue companies. Once a startup has meaningful revenue, like VidyaSetu, use Berkus as a sanity check rather than your main answer.

children.text: Method 2: The Scorecard Method

Popularised by angel investor Bill Payne, the scorecard method starts with a market reference: the average pre-money valuation of comparable seed-stage startups in the same region and sector. You then score the target against that average on weighted factors and adjust.

body.caption: A score of 100% means "the same as the average comparable startup"

children.text: Assume comparable seed-stage edtech startups have recently raised at an average pre-money valuation of ₹6 crore.

body.caption: Scorecard valuation of VidyaSetu (average comparable pre-money: ₹6 crore)

children.text: Pre-money valuation = ₹6 crore × 1.14 = ₹6.84 crore. VidyaSetu scores above average on team and market size, below average on competition and channels, and ends up about 14% above the typical comparable.

body.text: The scorecard method is only as good as its starting average. If the ₹6 crore average was taken from rounds in the 2021 boom, every result built on it is inflated. Always ask when and where the comparable average came from.

body.title: What matters most?
body.question: In the standard scorecard weights, which factor carries the most weight?
body.explanation: Team strength carries up to 30%, the largest single weight. At seed stage, the product and market usually change a great deal, so investors are mainly betting on the people who will navigate those changes.

children.text: Method 3: The Venture Capital Method

The VC method, set out by Harvard Business School professor William Sahlman, works backwards from an exit. Estimate what the company could be worth when investors sell, decide what return you need, and calculate what you can afford to pay today.

stats.label: Projected revenue in year 7
stats.context: Founder's plan, heavily discounted by the investor

stats.label: Target return
stats.context: Typical seed-stage expectation to offset failures

body.latex: \text{Post-money today} = \frac{\text{Exit value}}{\text{Target return multiple}} = \frac{₹240 \text{ crore}}{20} = ₹12 \text{ crore}
body.caption: The simple VC method, before adjusting for future dilution

children.text: That gives a post-money valuation of ₹12 crore and a pre-money valuation of ₹10 crore. But this ignores something you learned in Chapter 1: future rounds will dilute the seed investor before the exit.

body.title: Adjusting the VC method for future dilution

children.text: Suppose Series A, Series B and a new ESOP pool will together shrink the seed investor's stake to half of what it buys today. In other words, the investor retains 50% of its ownership by exit.
Ownership needed at exit.
To turn ₹2 crore into 20x, or ₹40 crore, from a ₹240 crore exit: ₹40 crore ÷ ₹240 crore = 16.67%.
Ownership needed today.
If only 50% of the stake survives: 16.67% ÷ 0.5 = 33.33%.
Post-money today.
₹2 crore ÷ 33.33% = ₹6 crore.
Pre-money today.
₹6 crore minus ₹2 crore = ₹4 crore.
Accounting for dilution cuts the pre-money valuation from ₹10 crore to ₹4 crore. This is the single most common reason founders and investors disagree on VC method numbers.

body.caption: The VC method with dilution built in

body.title: Run the VC method
body.prompt: An investor puts ₹3 crore into a startup it believes can exit for ₹300 crore. It targets a 10x return and expects to keep 60% of its stake through future rounds. What post-money valuation can it accept today, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Ownership needed at exit = (₹3 crore × 10) ÷ ₹300 crore = 10%. Ownership needed today = 10% ÷ 0.6 = 16.67%. Post-money = ₹3 crore ÷ 16.67% = ₹18 crore, so pre-money is ₹15 crore.

children.text: Method 4: Comparables

The comparables method asks a simple question: what have similar startups recently raised at? For companies with revenue, investors usually express this as a multiple of annualised revenue, or annual recurring revenue (ARR) for subscription businesses.

body.caption: Recent seed rounds in vernacular edtech (fictional comparables)

children.text: Apply that 8x to 13.3x range to VidyaSetu's ₹90 lakh of annualised revenue and you get a post-money valuation of ₹7.2 crore to ₹12 crore. Subtract the ₹2 crore being raised and the pre-money range is ₹5.2 crore to ₹10 crore, with the median 10x multiple pointing to ₹7 crore.

In India, you can find comparable rounds on paid databases like Tracxn and Venture Intelligence, and in startup news outlets such as Entrackr and Inc42, which often report round sizes and share prices from Registrar of Companies filings. For later-stage startups, investors also look at listed new-age companies on NSE and BSE and apply a discount for the startup being private and illiquid.

body.label: Tracxn
body.description: A startup database covering Indian funding rounds, investors and sector activity. Useful for building a comparables set, though full access is paid.

body.text: Bad comparables are the most common valuation trick. A founder raising a seed round who points to a Series C unicorn in the same sector is not giving you a comparable. Match stage, sector, geography, revenue scale, growth rate and funding climate before you trust a multiple.

children.text: Putting the Methods Together
Here is what the four methods say about VidyaSetu's pre-money valuation.

body.title: VidyaSetu pre-money valuation by method (₹ crore)

children.text: The answers run from ₹3.3 crore to ₹10 crore, but most of them overlap between about ₹5 crore and ₹7 crore. Suppose the round closes at a ₹6 crore pre-money valuation. The seed fund invests ₹2 crore at ₹8 crore post-money and owns 25%. That price is not "correct". It is defensible, because several independent approaches support it.

columns.label: Berkus
points: Strength: fast and forces you to name risks
Weakness: arbitrary caps, ignores market conditions

columns.label: Scorecard
points: Best for: pre-revenue and very early revenue
Strength: anchored to real market pricing
Weakness: only as good as the comparable average

columns.label: VC method
points: Best for: any stage with a credible exit story
Strength: ties price directly to required returns
Weakness: exit value and dilution are big guesses

columns.label: Comparables
points: Strength: reflects what investors are actually paying
Weakness: easily distorted by cherry-picked or stale deals

body.title: The VC method in one line
body.textWithBlank: In the simple VC method, post-money valuation equals expected exit value divided by the investor's target return ___.
body.explanation: A ₹240 crore exit and a 20x target multiple give a ₹12 crore post-money valuation, before adjusting for future dilution.

body.title: The unicorn comparable
body.scenario: A Hyderabad fintech founder raising a ₹1.5 crore seed round asks for a ₹40 crore pre-money valuation. Their justification: "A listed fintech trades at 10x revenue, and a Series C lending startup just raised at 15x revenue. We have ₹2 crore of annualised revenue and will reach ₹4 crore next year, so ₹40 crore is only 10x next year's revenue. That is conservative."
body.prompt: What is wrong with this reasoning, and how would you build a fairer comparables range?
body.modelAnswer:
Problems with the reasoning:
1. Wrong stage. A listed company and a Series C startup have years of data, scale and lower failure risk. Their multiples do not apply to a seed round.
2. Moving target. The founder applies a multiple to next year's projected revenue while quoting comparables based on current revenue. That mixes forward and trailing numbers.
3. The multiple is higher, not lower. On current revenue, ₹40 crore is 20x, above both the listed company and the Series C startup. A seed startup should usually get a lower multiple than later-stage or listed companies, to reflect risk and illiquidity.
4. Cherry-picking. Two hand-picked comparables are not a data set.

A fairer approach:
1. Find at least five to ten recent seed rounds in Indian fintech with similar revenue scale, using Tracxn, Venture Intelligence or ROC-based reporting.
2. Use the same revenue basis for every company, preferably current annualised revenue.
3. Take the median multiple, not the highest.
4. Cross-check with the scorecard and VC methods before accepting any number.

body.title: Triangulating a valuation you have been offered
steps: Ask the founders how they arrived at their number, and which method they used.
Run at least two methods yourself, one of which should be comparables if the startup has revenue.
Check that every comparable matches on stage, sector, revenue scale and funding climate.
In any VC method calculation, include realistic dilution from future rounds and ESOP top-ups.
Chart the range from each method and look for where they overlap.
Treat anything well above the overlap as a reason to negotiate or walk away.

cards.definition: Assigns capped values to five risk-reducing elements: idea, product, team, relationships and rollout. Built for pre-revenue startups.
Adjusts the average pre-money valuation of comparable startups using weighted scores for team, market, product and other factors.
Works backwards from expected exit value and target return to find the post-money valuation an investor can accept today.
The share of an investor's current ownership expected to survive future dilution until exit.
Valuation divided by annualised revenue, used to compare startups with revenue.
Annual recurring revenue: the yearly value of subscription or contracted repeat revenue.
Running several valuation methods and focusing on the range where their results overlap.

points: Early-stage valuation uses several simple, subjective methods, not one precise formula.
Berkus assigns capped values to five risk-reducing elements and suits pre-revenue startups.
Scorecard adjusts a market-average valuation using weighted factors, with team strength weighted most.
The VC method works back from exit value and target return. Ignoring future dilution can overstate the valuation by more than double.
Comparables reflect real deals but are easily distorted by mismatched stages, stale rounds and cherry-picking.
Run several methods, look for overlap, and use that range to negotiate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. VidyaSetu and all comparable startups shown are fictional, and the Berkus caps, scorecard average and return targets are illustrative. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
